questions.question: According to the periodization table of medieval Europe, the Early Middle Ages came to an end in which year?

solution_steps.title: Recall the three medieval periods
solution_steps.detail: The chapter table divides the Middle Ages into three blocks: Early Middle Ages (476-1000 C.E.), High Middle Ages (1000-1300 C.E.) and Late Middle Ages (1300-1450 C.E.).

solution_steps.title: Test each option against the table
solution_steps.detail: Option A (476 C.E.) is the year the Early Middle Ages began, not ended. Option C (1300 C.E.) is the close of the High Middle Ages. Option D (1450 C.E.) is the close of the Late Middle Ages.

solution_steps.title: Read off the correct boundary
solution_steps.detail: The table marks the Early Middle Ages as '476-1000 C.E.', so the period ended in 1000 C.E., when the High Middle Ages opened. The correct choice is B.

questions.answer: B. 1000 C.E. The Early Middle Ages ran from 476 to 1000 C.E., the period of Germanic invasions, the rise of the Frankish Kingdom and the emergence of feudalism.

similar_questions.question: According to the periodization table of medieval Europe, the Late Middle Ages came to an end in which year?
similar_questions.answer: D. 1450 C.E. The Late Middle Ages are given in the table as 1300-1450 C.E., the period of the Black Death, the Hundred Years' War and economic and demographic crisis.

solution_steps.title: Recall the Late Middle Ages entry
solution_steps.detail: The chapter table lists the Late Middle Ages as 1300-1450 C.E. with the Black Death and the Hundred Years' War as its key characteristics.

solution_steps.title: Compare the end dates in the options
solution_steps.detail: 1000 C.E. ends the Early Middle Ages and 1300 C.E. ends the High Middle Ages, so both describe other periods. 1347 C.E. is the year the Black Death arrived, not the end of the period.

solution_steps.title: Select the matching boundary
solution_steps.detail: Only 1450 C.E. matches the closing date of the Late Middle Ages, so the correct choice is D.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question asks for the end of the Early Middle Ages (1000 C.E.); this variant asks for the end of the Late Middle Ages (1450 C.E.) and uses a different distractor set that mixes period boundaries with the Black Death arrival year.

similar_questions.question: The High Middle Ages, known for the agricultural revolution, urbanization and the first universities, are dated by the chapter as 1000-1300 C.E. How many years long was that period?

solution_steps.title: Take the two boundary dates
solution_steps.detail: Start date = 1000 C.E. and end date = 1300 C.E., as given in the chapter's periodization table for the High Middle Ages.

solution_steps.title: Subtract end minus start
solution_steps.detail: Duration = end date - start date = 1300 - 1000 = 300.

solution_steps.title: State the conclusion
solution_steps.detail: The High Middle Ages lasted 300 years, the span in which feudalism peaked, towns grew and universities were founded in Bologna, Paris and Oxford.

similar_questions.variant_note: Instead of identifying a boundary year, this variant turns the same periodization row into a duration computation and requires the label of the High Middle Ages rather than the Early or Late Middle Ages.

questions.question: In the feudal contract of medieval Europe, what did the lord give to the vassal, and what did the vassal give to the lord in return?

solution_steps.title: Define vassalage
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that at the heart of feudalism was vassalage: local lords offered protection and granted land (a fief) to vassals (knights) in exchange for military service and loyalty.

solution_steps.title: List the lord's obligations
solution_steps.detail: The lord provided two things: protection, and a grant of land called a fief. The fief was the material reward that let the knight maintain himself and his equipment.

solution_steps.title: List the vassal's obligations
solution_steps.detail: The vassal (knight) repaid the lord with military service and loyalty. These two obligations made the grant of land a two-way, binding agreement rather than a gift.

solution_steps.title: Connect to the wider hierarchy
solution_steps.detail: Because kings could no longer protect their people from Viking, Magyar and Muslim invasions, this land-for-service exchange spread as a decentralized socio-economic and political system, with serfs at the bottom of the hierarchy providing labour on the lord's manor.

questions.answer: The lord granted the vassal land (a fief) and offered protection; in return the vassal owed the lord military service and loyalty.

similar_questions.question: Who stood at the bottom of the feudal hierarchy described in the chapter, and what did that group provide to the lord?
similar_questions.answer: The serfs. They were peasants legally tied to the land and they provided labour for the lord's manor.

solution_steps.title: Identify the lowest feudal rank
solution_steps.detail: The chapter describes the feudal hierarchy as ending at the bottom with the serfs: 'At the bottom of this hierarchy were the serfs.'

solution_steps.title: State the legal condition of serfs
solution_steps.detail: Serfs were peasants who were legally tied to the land, so they could not simply leave the manor as free workers could.

solution_steps.title: State their economic role
solution_steps.detail: Their function was to provide labour for the lord's manor, which made the manor and the whole feudal economy productive. Hence the answer: serfs, who supplied labour.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question examines the obligations between lord and vassal; this variant moves to the bottom rung of the same hierarchy and asks about serfs and their labour obligation instead.

similar_questions.question: Why did feudalism emerge in Western Europe during the Early Middle Ages?
similar_questions.answer: Because constant invasions by Vikings, Magyars and Muslims created extreme instability, and kings could no longer protect their people, so a new decentralized socio-economic and political system called feudalism emerged.

solution_steps.title: State the setting
solution_steps.detail: After the collapse of the Western Roman Empire in the late 5th century, Europe lacked a strong central government, and Germanic tribes established regional kingdoms.

solution_steps.title: Name the pressure
solution_steps.detail: During the Early Middle Ages (476-1000 C.E.) constant invasions by Vikings, Magyars and Muslims created extreme instability.

solution_steps.title: Identify the failure of royal protection
solution_steps.detail: Since kings could no longer protect their people, the population turned to local lords for security.

solution_steps.title: Draw the conclusion
solution_steps.detail: That vacuum of central protection produced a new decentralized socio-economic and political system called feudalism, built on vassalage, fiefs and serf labour.

similar_questions.variant_note: Instead of listing the obligations inside one feudal contract, this variant asks for the historical cause that produced feudalism in the first place, using the invasion and loss-of-protection logic of the chapter.

questions.question: Complete the sentence with the correct word: During the medieval era, monasteries became vital centres of education, literacy and political power, and the monks and nuns living there dedicated their lives to God while preserving ancient ______.

solution_steps.title: Locate the statement in the chapter
solution_steps.detail: The chapter says: 'Monasteries became vital centers of education, literacy, and political power. Monks and nuns dedicated their lives to God, preserving ancient texts and converting populations.'

solution_steps.title: Identify the missing object
solution_steps.detail: The thing that monasteries and their inhabitants preserved is identified in the text as 'ancient texts' - that is, written documents from earlier ages, including Roman and Christian learning.

solution_steps.title: Check that the word fits the grammar
solution_steps.detail: The blank follows the adjective 'ancient' and is the direct object of 'preserving', so a plural noun is required; 'texts' fits both the meaning and the grammar.

solution_steps.title: Confirm the historical point
solution_steps.detail: This preservation work is why the chapter describes the Catholic Church and its monasteries as a unifying influence of the medieval era, alongside converting populations.

questions.answer: texts. Monasteries were vital centres of education, literacy and political power, and monks and nuns preserved ancient texts.

similar_questions.question: Complete the sentence with the correct word: The Catholic Church's dispute with monarchs over the appointment of church officials was finally settled by the ______ of Worms in 1122.
similar_questions.answer: Concordat. The conflict between the Church and monarchs over the appointment of church officials was settled by the Concordat of Worms in 1122.

solution_steps.title: Recall the Church-monarch conflict
solution_steps.detail: The chapter explains that the Catholic Church established a complicated relationship with monarchs, producing conflicts over the appointment of church officials.

solution_steps.title: Find the settlement
solution_steps.detail: The text states that this conflict was 'eventually settled by the Concordat of Worms in 1122'.

solution_steps.title: Insert the missing term
solution_steps.detail: The blank precedes 'of Worms in 1122', so the missing word is the name of the agreement: Concordat.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question completes a statement about monasteries preserving ancient texts; this variant completes a statement about the Concordat of Worms, shifting the tested fact from Church learning to Church-State conflict.

similar_questions.question: Complete the sentence with the correct word: Emperor Justinian is celebrated for his massive building projects, most notably the ______, a masterpiece of architectural engineering that served as the grandest church in Christendom.
similar_questions.answer: Hagia Sophia. Justinian's most notable building project was the Hagia Sophia, which served as the grandest church in Christendom.

solution_steps.title: Recall Justinian's reign
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that under Emperor Justinian (527-565 C.E.) the Eastern Roman Empire briefly reconquered much of the Mediterranean, including Italy and North Africa.

solution_steps.title: Identify his building programme
solution_steps.detail: Justinian 'is also celebrated for his massive building projects, most notably the Hagia Sophia, a masterpiece of architectural engineering'.

solution_steps.title: Fill the blank and confirm its role
solution_steps.detail: The missing name is the Hagia Sophia, which the chapter says served as the grandest church in Christendom. The correct completion is therefore 'Hagia Sophia'.

similar_questions.variant_note: This variant moves from Western Europe to the Byzantine Empire, completing a sentence about Justinian's Hagia Sophia rather than about monastic text preservation.

questions.question: A Grade 10 history group in Asmara is studying the Black Death of 1347. Their textbook states that the plague wiped out an estimated 38 million people in Europe, which was roughly half of Europe's population at that time. (a) Work out the size of Europe's population before the plague arrived in 1347. (b) Work out how many Europeans survived the plague. (c) State the percentage of the pre-plague population that survived.

solution_steps.title: Identify the given data and set up notation
solution_steps.detail: Let P be Europe's population before the plague. The chapter gives: deaths D = 38 million, and the deaths were roughly half of the population, that is D = 1/2 x P, or equivalently D = 0.5P.

solution_steps.title: Choose the relation that links deaths and population
solution_steps.detail: Since the death toll equals half of the whole population, the whole population is twice the death toll. The working relation is P = D / 0.5, which is the same as P = 2D.

solution_steps.title: Substitute the value for D
solution_steps.detail: Substituting D = 38 million into P = 2D gives P = 2 x 38 million = 76 million people.

solution_steps.title: Find the number of survivors
solution_steps.detail: Survivors = pre-plague population - deaths = 76 million - 38 million = 38 million people. Notice that survivors and deaths are equal here, which is exactly what 'roughly half died' means.

solution_steps.title: Convert the survivors into a percentage
solution_steps.detail: Percentage surviving = (survivors / pre-plague population) x 100 = (38 million / 76 million) x 100 = 0.5 x 100 = 50%.

solution_steps.title: Check the answer and state its historical meaning
solution_steps.detail: Check: 50% of 76 million = 38 million, which matches the recorded death toll, so the arithmetic is consistent. Historically, this huge loss of roughly half of Europe's population disrupted the feudal economy, because the labour force that worked the manors was drastically reduced.

questions.answer: (a) Europe's pre-plague population was about 76 million people (2 x 38 million). (b) About 38 million Europeans survived. (c) The survivors were 50% of the pre-plague population.

similar_questions.question: In a medieval port city on the trade routes that carried the Black Death in 1347, an estimated 1,600 people died of the plague, which was roughly half of the city's population. (a) What was the city's population before the plague? (b) How many people survived?
similar_questions.answer: (a) The city's population before the plague was 3,200 people (2 x 1,600). (b) 1,600 people survived.

solution_steps.title: Set up the given relation
solution_steps.detail: Let C be the city's pre-plague population. Deaths = 1,600 and deaths were roughly half the population, so 1,600 = 0.5C.

solution_steps.title: Solve for the pre-plague population
solution_steps.detail: Rearranging 1,600 = 0.5C gives C = 1,600 / 0.5 = 3,200 people.

solution_steps.title: Work out the survivors
solution_steps.detail: Survivors = C - deaths = 3,200 - 1,600 = 1,600 people.

solution_steps.title: Check against the stated fraction
solution_steps.detail: Half of 3,200 is 1,600, which matches both the death toll and the survivor count, so the result is consistent. This mirrors the chapter's statement that the Black Death wiped out roughly half of Europe's population.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question works at the scale of all Europe with a death toll of 38 million; this variant scales the same halving relationship down to a single Italian trade-route port city with a death toll of 1,600, and it drops the percentage part while keeping the same two-step reasoning.

similar_questions.question: In a Byzantine province in 1347, 4,200 people died in a plague outbreak, which was roughly 30% of the province's population. (a) Work out the province's population before the outbreak. (b) Work out how many people survived. (c) State the percentage that survived. (Note: work carefully with the 30% figure.)
similar_questions.answer: (a) The pre-outbreak population was 14,000 people. (b) 9,800 people survived. (c) 70% of the population survived.

solution_steps.title: Translate the percentage into a decimal
solution_steps.detail: 30% = 30/100 = 0.3, so the deaths equal 0.3 of the population: 4,200 = 0.3 x P, where P is the pre-outbreak population.

solution_steps.title: Compute the survivors
solution_steps.detail: Survivors = P - deaths = 14,000 - 4,200 = 9,800 people.

solution_steps.title: Convert survivors to a percentage
solution_steps.detail: Percentage surviving = 100% - 30% = 70%, since everyone either died or survived. Check: 70% of 14,000 = 0.7 x 14,000 = 9,800, which agrees with step 3.

solution_steps.title: Note the trap and the historical point
solution_steps.detail: A common error is to treat 4,200 as more than half the population or to divide by 30 instead of 0.3; dividing by 0.3 correctly gives 14,000. The example shows how a plague could remove a large share of a region's people and so reduce the labour force that the feudal economy depended on.

similar_questions.variant_note: This variant keeps the same structure of finding a pre-plague population from a death toll, but changes the fraction from one half to 30%, adds the surviving-percentage step back in, and moves the setting from Western Europe to a Byzantine province.

questions.question: Using the figures and events of the Late Middle Ages in the chapter, analyse the combined impact of the Black Death and the Hundred Years' War on Western Europe. Your answer must: (a) state what happened to Europe's population after the Black Death and what that did to the feudal economy; (b) state the duration of the Hundred Years' War from its given start and end years; (c) explain the final consequence that the chapter says the war produced for European political life; and (d) explain why a war that caused massive economic damage could still leave a positive political legacy.

solution_steps.title: Establish the scale of the Black Death
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the Black Death, a bubonic plague, arrived in 1347 via Italian trade routes and wiped out an estimated 38 million people, roughly half of Europe's population. The demographic collapse was therefore of the order of a 50% loss.

solution_steps.title: Trace the economic consequence of that loss
solution_steps.detail: Because the population fell by roughly half, the supply of peasants and serfs who provided labour on the manors fell with it. The chapter says this demographic collapse 'disrupted the feudal economy' - the manorial system that rested on serf labour and on the lord's manor could no longer function as before.

solution_steps.title: Compute the duration of the Hundred Years' War
solution_steps.detail: Duration = end year - start year = 1453 - 1337. Working the subtraction: 1453 - 1300 = 153, and 1337 - 1300 = 37, so 1453 - 1337 = 153 - 37 = 116. The Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years.

solution_steps.title: State the war's economic cost
solution_steps.detail: The chapter records that this long war between France and England caused massive economic damage, which combined with the Black Death to deepen the crisis of the Late Middle Ages (1300-1450 C.E.).

solution_steps.title: Identify the political legacy
solution_steps.detail: Despite the damage, the war 'ultimately sparked a sense of national identity, exemplified by figures like Joan of Arc', the teenage peasant girl who led the French army to victory at Orleans before being captured and burned at the stake by the English.

solution_steps.title: Reconcile the destruction with the positive legacy
solution_steps.detail: The two effects are not contradictory. Wars of survival forced people in France and England to identify with king and country rather than with a local lord, and the shared suffering created a common bond. At the same time the Black Death and the war together weakened the feudal nobility, which the chapter says prepared the way for the end of the Middle Ages and the strengthening of national monarchs.

solution_steps.title: Draw the overall conclusion
solution_steps.detail: Combined verdict: demographically, Europe lost roughly half its people to plague from 1347; economically, the feudal/manorial system was disrupted and both kingdoms were damaged by 116 years of war; politically, the crisis destroyed the old feudal order and gave birth to national identity and stronger national monarchies - the doorway out of the Middle Ages.

questions.answer: (a) The Black Death (arriving 1347) killed an estimated 38 million people, roughly half of Europe's population, and that demographic collapse disrupted the feudal economy, which depended on serf labour on the manor. (b) The Hundred Years' War lasted 1453 - 1337 = 116 years. (c) It ultimately sparked a sense of national identity, exemplified by Joan of Arc. (d) Because the war made people identify with king and country instead of their local lord, and the war and plague together weakened the feudal nobility, strengthening national monarchs and preparing the end of the Middle Ages.

similar_questions.question: The Black Death arrived in Europe in 1347, and the medieval period described in the chapter closes in 1500 C.E. (a) Work out how many years separated the arrival of the plague from the end of the medieval period. (b) The plague itself is described as a bubonic plague spread along trade routes; explain why the chapter says this event 'disrupted the feudal economy'. (c) Name the period (476-1000, 1000-1300 or 1300-1450 C.E.) in which the plague struck, and give one other major crisis the chapter places in that same period.
similar_questions.answer: (a) 1500 - 1347 = 153 years. (b) Because it killed roughly half of Europe's population, removing the serfs and peasants whose labour sustained the manor, so the feudal economy could no longer work as before. (c) The Late Middle Ages (1300-1450 C.E.); the other major crisis of that period is the Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) between France and England.

solution_steps.title: Explain the economic disruption
solution_steps.detail: The chapter records that the plague wiped out an estimated 38 million people, roughly half of Europe's population, and that this demographic collapse disrupted the feudal economy. The mechanism is labour: serfs were legally tied to the land and provided the labour for the lord's manor, so halving the population starved the manorial system of workers.

solution_steps.title: Place the plague in the correct period
solution_steps.detail: 1347 falls between 1300 and 1450, so the Black Death belongs to the Late Middle Ages (1300-1450 C.E.).

solution_steps.title: Add the parallel crisis
solution_steps.detail: The chapter's table lists two key characteristics for the Late Middle Ages: the Black Death and the Hundred Years' War, alongside economic and demographic crisis. The second event is therefore the Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) between France and England.

similar_questions.variant_note: This variant drops the multi-part synthesis of plague plus war and instead asks for a date-difference calculation (1347 to 1500), a one-event causal explanation of economic disruption, and a period-classification task, making the scope narrower while still covering two chapter facts.

similar_questions.question: A study group in Keren is asked to judge how a long war can end in defeat for a cause yet still leave a nation stronger in identity. Apply this to the Crusades: (a) state the primary objective the Crusades failed to achieve and the year in which the First Crusade did capture Jerusalem; (b) explain how the Crusades still revived European trade and helped end feudalism. Then compare this with the Hundred Years' War, which caused massive economic damage but sparked national identity.
similar_questions.answer: (a) The primary objective was to hold the Holy Land (Jerusalem) against Muslim control; the First Crusade did capture Jerusalem in 1099, but by the end of the 13th century the Western crusaders had been completely driven out of the Middle East. (b) The Crusades stimulated massive trade between Europe and the Middle East, enriching Italian port cities such as Venice and Genoa, and they weakened the feudal nobility because many lords died or went bankrupt fighting, which strengthened national monarchs. The comparison: in both cases a costly military effort failed to secure its original goal, yet it produced an unintended structural gain - trade and stronger monarchy for the Crusades, national identity for the Hundred Years' War.

solution_steps.title: State the Crusades' goal and the 1099 success
solution_steps.detail: In 1095 Pope Urban II called the First Crusade, urging European Christians to march east and reclaim the Holy Land (Jerusalem) from Muslim control. The First Crusade successfully captured Jerusalem in 1099 and established several Crusader states.

solution_steps.title: Show that the objective ultimately failed
solution_steps.detail: In 1187 Saladin recaptured Jerusalem, and by the end of the 13th century the Western crusaders had been completely driven out of the Middle East, so the primary objective was not held.

solution_steps.title: Explain the unintended economic gain
solution_steps.detail: Though they failed militarily, the Crusades stimulated massive trade between Europe and the Middle East, leading to the growth of wealthy Italian port cities like Venice and Genoa.

solution_steps.title: Explain the unintended political gain
solution_steps.detail: The Crusades weakened the feudal nobility, since many lords died or went bankrupt fighting, and this ultimately strengthened the power of national monarchs, paving the way for the end of the Middle Ages.

solution_steps.title: Build the comparison with the Hundred Years' War
solution_steps.detail: The pattern is the same in both cases: a long and destructive conflict fails to secure its original objective, yet it breaks the grip of the feudal nobility and creates a larger loyalty. For the Crusades that loyalty is to wealth, trade and stronger monarchs; for the Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) it is national identity, exemplified by Joan of Arc. Neither conflict was a straightforward victory, and both accelerated the end of the Middle Ages.

similar_questions.variant_note: This variant keeps the analytical 'destructive conflict with an unintended positive legacy' reasoning of the main question but transfers it from the Late Middle Ages (Black Death and Hundred Years' War) to the Crusades, adds the specific dates 1095, 1099 and 1187, and requires an explicit comparison between the two cases.
